extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants, patent attorneys, and agents involved in prosecution and enablement/written-description analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification enables the full scope of claimed subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 112(a), including how to treat examples, prophetic examples, genus claims, predictability of the art, examiner burdens, and applicant rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable correlation between in vitro and in vivo activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A rigorous or an invariable exact correlation is not required; based upon the relevant evidence as a whole, there need only be a reasonable correlation between the disclosed in vitro utility and an in vivo activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the disclosure of pharmacological activity is reasonable based upon the probative evidence, a rigorous correlation is not necessary (citing Cross v. Iizuka). Examiner should evaluate the evidence as a whole when assessing the sufficiency of correlation for utility/enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working examples and claimed genus
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claimed genus, representative examples together with a statement applicable to the genus as a whole will ordinarily be sufficient if one skilled in the art would expect the claimed genus could be used in that manner without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of enablement for other members of the genus is required only where the examiner advances adequate reasons to establish that a person skilled in the art could not use the genus as a whole without undue experimentation. In some instances a few examples plus disclosure of a 'general quality ... running through' the class may suffice (citing Amgen v. Sanofi and Incandescent Lamp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic examples must not be represented as actual
rubrics_metrics.description: When prophetic examples are described ambiguously or in a manner that implies results are actual, the adequacy and accuracy of the disclosure may be questioned and can give rise to enablement and/or written description issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prophetic examples reasonably raise questions whether results are actual, examiners should consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and/or written description guidance (MPEP §§ 2164, 2163). Applicant should respond with actual test results or with arguments/declaration evidence showing strong reason to believe predicted results, being careful not to introduce new matter. Misrepresenting prophetic examples in past tense can raise inequitable conduct issues (citing Hoffmann‑La Roche v. Promega; Apotex v. UCB). See also MPEP § 2004, item 8: no results should be represented as actual unless actually achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability of the art inversely affects required disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of guidance or direction needed to enable the invention is inversely related to the amount of knowledge in the state of the art and the predictability in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When more is known and the art is predictable, less must be explicitly stated in the specification. Nascent or unpredictable technology requires more specific and useful teaching (citing In re Fisher; Chiron v. Genentech). Examiner should assess what one skilled in the art could extrapolate from the disclosure and prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of required enablement varies with predictability (single species vs genus)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single embodiment may provide broad enablement in predictable arts (e.g., mechanical/electrical), but in unpredictable arts (e.g., many chemical reactions, physiological activity) the disclosure of a single species usually does not provide adequate basis to support generic claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the predictable/unpredictable nature of the art when evaluating whether disclosure of one species enables the full claimed genus. Case law examples include In re Vickers, In re Cook, In re Soll, In re Fisher, and related decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must construe claims and establish a reasonable basis to question enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before any enablement analysis, the examiner must construe the claims and, for ambiguous terms, select and explicitly state the meaning intended to be used in examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make an enablement rejection, the examiner has the initial burden to establish a reasonable basis to question enablement and explain why the disclosure is doubted (citing Genentech v. Wellcome; In re Wright; In re Marzocchi). The examiner must back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning inconsistent with the contested statements and provide specific technical reasons (In re Bowen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's analysis must consider all enablement factors and the evidence as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to conclude a disclosure is not enabling based on analysis of only one factor; the examiner’s analysis must consider all the evidence related to each enablement factor and base conclusions on the evidence as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explanation of rejection should focus on the factors, reasons, and evidence that lead to the conclusion of non‑enablement, making specific findings of fact supported by evidence and drawing conclusions therefrom. References should be supplied if possible to support a prima facie case (citing In re Wands, In re Marzocchi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution: present best case in first Office action and identify allowable subject matter early
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with compact prosecution, if an enablement rejection is appropriate the first Office action on the merits should present the best case with all relevant reasons, issues, and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing the best rejection in the first action allows applicant to rebut and prevents unnecessary follow-up and expansion that could delay finality. If examiner recognizes limitations that would render claims enabled, the examiner should note such limitations to applicant early and identify enabled, allowable subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement determinations are based on the evidence as a whole; applicant's burden to rebut
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examiner establishes a reasonable basis to question enablement, the burden falls on applicant to present persuasive arguments, supported by suitable proofs where necessary, that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention using the application as a guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant's evidence need not be absolute but must be convincing by a preponderance of the evidence. Declarations or affidavits under 37 C.F.R. § 1.132 are evidence but their weight depends on factual support (citing In re Brandstadter; In re Buchner; In re Alton). Examiner must weigh specification, applicant‑supplied evidence, and evidence relied on in the rejection and decide based on the evidence, not personal opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be enabling as of the filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is assessed as of the filing date and requires consideration of the nature of the invention, the state of the prior art, and the level of skill in the art at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State of the art is what one skilled in the art would have known at filing. Post‑filing publications generally cannot be used to demonstrate enablement except in limited circumstances (citing Chiron v. Genentech; In re Gunn; In re Budnick; In re Hogan; In re Wright). The specification need not disclose what is well‑known to those skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable persons skilled in the relevant arts (including multiple arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where different arts are involved, the specification is enabling if it enables persons skilled in each art to carry out the aspect of the invention applicable to their specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two distinct technologies are relevant, disclosure is adequate if a person of ordinary skill in each technology could practice the invention from the disclosures (citing In re Naquin; Technicon Instruments v. Alpkem; Ex parte Zechnall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of experimentation / undue experimentation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation to make and use a claimed invention; reasonableness depends on the nature of the invention and the underlying art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the Wands factors: the quantity, quality, and predictability of guidance; time and expense; routine nature of experiments; necessity of difficult assays; and whether extensive screening is required. Time and expense are factors but not controlling. Examples: Telectronics (time/expense alone not undue), Amgen v. Sanofi (need to screen millions of antibodies deemed undue), In re Ghiron (functional block diagrams insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: When missing essential information, examiner should identify what is missing and why
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubt about enablement commonly arises because information is missing about one or more essential claim elements or relationships between elements which one skilled in the art could not develop without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and explain why that information is needed to provide enablement. This includes pinpointing essential parts or relationships and supplying references if possible to support a prima facie case (see MPEP § 2164.06(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement serves to prevent claims broader than disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement ensures adequate disclosure and prevents claims broader than the disclosed invention; broad claim language is used at the peril of losing any claim that cannot be enabled across its full scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should be mindful that overly broad functional language or genus claims that extend beyond what the specification enables can be rejected for lack of enablement; the specification must teach how to make and use the claimed subject matter commensurate with claim scope (examples and case law referenced).
